group.passage: In AD 79, the volcano Mount Vesuvius erupted and buried the Roman town of Pompeii. In the texts below, a science writer describes what archaeologists have learned from the ruins, and a guide who works at the site explains what visitors often get wrong.

passage_parts.label: A
passage_parts.title: What the Ash Kept
passage_parts.text: When Vesuvius erupted, ash and small stones rained down on Pompeii for hours, and a cloud of scorching gas then swept through its streets. The town disappeared so completely that it was largely forgotten until systematic digging began in 1748. What the ash protected is remarkable: brightly painted walls, graffiti scratched by ordinary residents, and even loaves of bread left in a bakery oven, turned to charcoal by the heat. In the 1860s, the archaeologist Giuseppe Fiorelli noticed hollow spaces in the hardened ash where bodies had slowly decayed. By pouring plaster into these spaces, he created lifelike figures of victims in their final moments. Recently, though, DNA taken from several of the figures has posed a serious challenge to versions of their stories that had been repeated for generations. One adult wearing a gold bracelet and holding a child, long described as a mother, turned out to be a man who was not related to the child at all.

passage_parts.label: B
passage_parts.title: Notes from a Pompeii Guide
passage_parts.text: Many visitors arrive expecting a town stopped in mid-step, as though everyone had frozen in place the moment the ash began to fall. I tell them the truth is messier. Many residents seem to have escaped during the first hours of the eruption, taking their valuables with them, and much of what remained has since been dug up, carried off or patched together by earlier excavators. Even the famous plaster figures have been repaired again and again over the years, so I ask visitors to take the touching stories about them with a grain of salt. Still, the town never fails to amaze. My favorite stop is a wall covered in painted election slogans, in which neighbors urge passers-by to vote for a candidate because he brings good bread. And about a third of Pompeii is still underground, waiting for archaeologists with better tools than ours.

translation_zh.text:
西元 79 年，維蘇威火山爆發，掩埋了羅馬城鎮龐貝。在下面兩篇短文中，一位科普作家描述考古學家從遺址中學到了什麼，一位在遺址工作的導覽員則說明遊客常常誤會了什麼。

A　火山灰留下了什麼
維蘇威火山爆發時，火山灰和小石塊在龐貝落了好幾個小時，接著一團灼熱的氣體席捲了街道。這座城鎮消失得如此徹底，以致於幾乎被世人遺忘，直到 1748 年才開始有系統的挖掘。火山灰保護下來的東西令人驚嘆：色彩鮮豔的壁畫、一般居民刻下的塗鴉，甚至還有留在麵包店烤爐裡、被高溫燒成木炭的一條條麵包。1860 年代，考古學家朱塞佩．菲奧雷利注意到，在硬化的火山灰中，遺體慢慢腐爛的地方留下了空洞。他把石膏灌進這些空洞，做出了受難者臨終時刻栩栩如生的人形。不過最近，從其中幾具人形取得的 DNA，對流傳了好幾代的說法提出了嚴重的挑戰。一位戴著金手環、抱著孩子、長久以來被描述為母親的成人，結果是一名和那個孩子毫無血緣關係的男性。

B　一位龐貝導覽員的筆記
許多遊客來的時候，以為會看到一座停在半步之間的城鎮，好像每個人都在火山灰開始落下的那一刻定格了。我告訴他們，真實情況要混亂得多。許多居民似乎在噴發的最初幾個小時就逃走了，還帶走了貴重物品；而留下來的東西，後來有很多又被早期的挖掘者挖出、搬走，或東拼西湊地修補。就連那些著名的石膏人形，多年來也一再被修補，所以我請遊客對關於它們的動人故事保留看待。儘管如此，這座城鎮總是令人驚嘆。我最喜歡的一站是一面寫滿選舉標語的牆，鄰居們在標語中呼籲路人投票給某位候選人，因為他「帶來好麵包」。此外，龐貝大約還有三分之一埋在地底下，等待擁有比我們更好工具的考古學家。
